title: Planning for a renewables-led grid: risks from Dunkelflaute, storage and interconnectors
label: 28 October 2026 · Dunkelflaute, intermittency and storage
summary: Ofgem’s engineering director, Peter Bingham, told the Lords committee that Britain is moving to a renewables-led system and recognised the supply risks that brings. He explained the current reliability standard for electricity, how capacity modelling treats imports, and why long-duration storage and network connections remain priorities. Ofgem has launched initial schemes for long-duration energy storage and interconnectors, will learn from the first round, and plans further consultations and close work with government and networks to remove barriers.

speakers.label: Peter Bingham
speakers.name: Peter Bingham
speakers.role: Director for Engineering and Technology, Ofgem

glossary.definition: A weather period with very low wind and solar generation, creating sustained low renewable output.
High-voltage cables linking the UK electricity system to other countries so power can be imported or exported.
Long-duration energy storage: technologies that can store electricity for many hours or days.
National Electricity System Operator: the organisation that models demand, plans capacity and runs scenarios for the grid.
A probabilistic reliability standard showing how often a system might fail to meet demand under planning assumptions.
A regulatory support model Ofgem uses to give certain projects revenue certainty, with limits on what they can earn and lose.
Strategic Spatial Energy Plan: government-led plan setting the country’s needs for generation, storage and networks.
Central Strategic Network Plan: the planned national transmission network plan that follows the SSEP.
Security and Quality of Supply Standard: technical rules for operating the transmission system safely.

chapters.title: Who is speaking for system engineering?
chapters.takeaway: Ofgem has engineers in-house to judge technical risks and advise on network and storage planning.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Please introduce yourself for the record.

turns.speaker: Peter Bingham
turns.text: I'm Peter Bingham, Director for Engineering and Technology at Ofgem. I lead engineers who assess and regulate the technical side of the electricity system.

chapters.title: How we judge reliability today
chapters.takeaway: Electricity reliability is planned to a probabilistic standard, not a single 'one-in-X' worst case; NESO runs many scenarios to set required capacity.

turns.speaker: Lord Ashcombe
turns.text: How big a risk is rising reliance on weather-dependent generation to security of supply?

turns.speaker: Peter Bingham
turns.text: We recognise the risk. Renewables are intermittent, so we need dispatchable sources and storage to fill gaps and keep supply secure.

turns.speaker: Lord Ashcombe
turns.text: Is there an equivalent to gas's 'one-in-20-year' standard for electricity? What worst-case probability do you plan for?

turns.speaker: Peter Bingham
turns.text: Electricity planning uses the government's three-hour loss of load expectation, a probabilistic standard. NESO models tens of thousands of scenarios—different weather, generation and interconnector conditions—to decide needed capacity.

turns.speaker: Lord Ashcombe
turns.text: So there's no explicit 'one-in-50' or similar metric for electricity?

turns.speaker: Peter Bingham
turns.text: No. The approach is statistical: you have distributions of demand and supply and plan to cover the range where it’s value for money to do so.

chapters.title: Long-duration storage: current steps and limits
chapters.takeaway: Ofgem has opened mechanisms for long-duration storage but the first round focused on more mature technologies; work and consultations will follow for ultra-long solutions.

turns.speaker: Lord Krebs
turns.text: Why aren't you focused on ultra-long-duration storage (100+ hours) given Dunkelflaute risks?

turns.speaker: Peter Bingham
turns.text: The first LDES window sought technologies offering eight hours or more—some projects in the draft set reach about 30 hours. The scheme didn't exclude longer-duration tech, but it emphasised more mature technologies.

turns.speaker: Lord Krebs
turns.text: That sounds like 'watch this space'. What scale would be needed to cover days of low renewables?

turns.speaker: Peter Bingham
turns.text: Scale needs will be in the SSEP. There are many options—storage, hydrogen, CCUS, unabated gas, interconnection and demand response. Government will choose pathways and then mechanisms to deliver them.

turns.speaker: Earl Russell
turns.text: Is special thinking or a special mechanism needed for ultra-long storage?

turns.speaker: Peter Bingham
turns.text: Possibly. These projects are capital-intensive and nascent. There may be a case for dedicated support—similar to how CfD auctions had buckets for emergent tech—to seed such technologies.

turns.speaker: Baroness Whitaker
turns.text: Who will ensure storage choices are value for money and don't push up consumer bills?

turns.speaker: Peter Bingham
turns.text: SSEP pathways trade off affordability, security and emissions. Ofgem wants government to pick the lowest-cost pathway. LDES exists to lower market barriers; we will learn from the first window and consult on future design.

turns.speaker: Baroness Whitaker
turns.text: When will we see final determinations from the first LDES round?

turns.speaker: Peter Bingham
turns.text: We expect to announce results this year; I'll confirm timings in writing so the committee can include them in its report.

chapters.title: Interconnectors: benefits, limits and vulnerabilities
chapters.takeaway: Interconnectors lower costs and add diversity, but they're derated in planning and not a guaranteed backup if widespread shortages occur.

turns.speaker: Lord Rooker
turns.text: Interconnectors supplied 15% of power in 2025 and more are coming—how reliable are they in a Dunkelflaute or if cables are damaged?

turns.speaker: Peter Bingham
turns.text: Interconnectors give access to a wider market, let us export surplus renewables, and add diversity. NESO derates their contribution in capacity modelling so we don't rely on full import flows in tight scenarios.

turns.speaker: Lord Rooker
turns.text: But what if Europe faces the same weather and can't export? Or cables are disrupted?

turns.speaker: Peter Bingham
turns.text: That’s why domestic capacity and the capacity market are designed to fill gaps. Interconnectors are reliable historically, but not infallible; planning assumes contingencies.

turns.speaker: Lord Trees
turns.text: Can we check whether imports are actually low-carbon? Some bills claim 'low-carbon UK-only' supply.

turns.speaker: Peter Bingham
turns.text: Electricity traded across markets doesn't carry a colour label in that trading. UK suppliers can offer green-labelled UK-produced power, but imports are traded on European markets without that distinction.

turns.speaker: Baroness McIntosh of Pickering
turns.text: Would it help to land interconnectors on brownfield sites in London to strengthen London’s supply directly?

turns.speaker: Peter Bingham
turns.text: There’s no regulatory barrier—developers choose landing sites and technical feasibility matters. If it’s feasible, it could make sense operationally.

turns.speaker: Lord Ashcombe
turns.text: Do we have enough capacity domestically without interconnectors at winter peak?

turns.speaker: Peter Bingham
turns.text: It depends on renewable output; modelling accounts for low import scenarios. You can’t cover every imaginable extreme, but the plan aims for a reliable, diverse mix.

chapters.title: Regulatory blockers, standards and next steps
chapters.takeaway: Ofgem sees grid connections as the main barrier, will push faster network investment, learn from LDES, and follow up on technical standard changes.

turns.speaker: Earl Russell
turns.text: What regulatory barriers remain to deploying storage and low-carbon dispatchable power?

turns.speaker: Peter Bingham
turns.text: The dominant challenge is grid infrastructure and connections. Ofgem’s role is to fund and enable transmission companies to build at pace and to remove regulatory bottlenecks.

turns.speaker: Earl Russell
turns.text: What specific planning or regulatory actions are you taking?

turns.speaker: Peter Bingham
turns.text: After the SSEP, the Central Strategic Network Plan (CSNP) will set network investment needs. Ofgem will make sure funding and regulatory settings allow prompt delivery.

turns.speaker: Lord Redwood
turns.text: You approved some changes to voltage tolerances in the SQSS—can you write to us summarising recent NESO standard changes?

turns.speaker: Peter Bingham
turns.text: Yes. I wasn't familiar with all the specific documents you mentioned but we did approve widening some voltage tolerances recently; I will write with more detail on developments in standards.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Thank you. Please confirm LDES determinations timing and the details on the SQSS changes in writing.

turns.speaker: Peter Bingham
turns.text: I will. And we will share what we learn from the first LDES window and consult on future windows and design changes.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Thank you for your time and answers today.
